solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: British dished rupees out for such as Gunga Din

indicators.note: out says the rupees are put out of the word, so that letter goes
something dished has been knocked out of shape, so the remaining letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
R is the abbreviation for rupee(s)

explanation.surface: A British official hands out rupees to Kipling's famous water-carrier.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove R from BRITISH, leaving BITISH, then rearrange to BHISTI. 'British' looks like the usual B, but here the whole word is used.
explanation.definitionFit: A bhisti is an Indian water-carrier, and Kipling's Gunga Din is the regimental water-bearer of that trade.

clue.text: Brother embracing knight in devotion leading to salvation

indicators.note: embracing means holding something within one's arms, so the brother word wraps around the knight

blocks.note: bhai is Hindi for brother
KT is the abbreviation for knight

explanation.surface: A monk embraces a knight in a scene of religious devotion.
explanation.walkthrough: Bhai is Hindi for brother, fitting the Indian answer rather than the usual BRO or BR.
explanation.definitionFit: Bhakti is the Hindu path of loving devotion to a god, regarded as a route to salvation.

clue.text: Playwright promised Scotch, ultimate in usquebaugh, genuine

indicators.note: ultimate means last, so only the closing letter of the word is used

blocks.note: the final letter of usquebaugh
echt, from German, means genuine or authentic

explanation.surface: A dramatist was promised Scotch whisky, with a final dram of genuine usquebaugh.
explanation.walkthrough: Two definitions plus wordplay: Ben Hecht was an American playwright, and hecht is a Scots past tense of hight, 'promised'. Usquebaugh is Gaelic for whisky.
explanation.definitionFit: Ben Hecht wrote plays such as The Front Page, and in Scots dialect hecht means promised or offered.

clue.text: Met men's high altitude device yielding some facts on descending

indicators.note: yielding some means giving up just a part of the following words, so the answer lies within them

blocks.note: found running across the end of facts, all of on, and the start of descending

explanation.surface: Meteorologists' high-flying instrument sends back facts as it comes down.
explanation.walkthrough: Met men are meteorologists, from the Met Office, Britain's weather service.
explanation.definitionFit: A sonde is an instrument package sent aloft by balloon or rocket to measure atmospheric conditions for weather forecasters.

clue.text: Old hat? That's seen in test no longer

indicators.note: seen in places one thing inside another, so the old-hat word sits within the test word

blocks.note: that, referring back to old hat, is corn: trite, hackneyed material
trie is an obsolete spelling of try, a test

explanation.surface: A sceptic asks whether something is old hat because it no longer appears in the test.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old hat' does double duty: it is the definition, and 'That' refers back to it as the hackneyed stuff in the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: A tricorne is a three-cornered hat of the eighteenth century, literally an old hat.

clue.text: Like an attractive loan, boring apparently?

blocks.note: first meaning: a loan with no interest charged
second meaning, read literally: free of interest, so dull

explanation.walkthrough: 'apparently' flags the humorous literal reading of the phrase as lacking anything interesting.
explanation.definitionFit: A loan on which no charge is made is appealing to a borrower, while something devoid of interest is dull.

clue.text: Pages occupying perch bob up and down

indicators.note: occupying means taking up space inside something, so the pages go within the perch

blocks.note: a perch or pole is an old unit of length
PP is the abbreviation for pages

explanation.surface: Pageboys sitting on a perch bounce up and down.
explanation.walkthrough: Perch, pole and rod are all names for the same old measure of length, five and a half yards.
explanation.definitionFit: To popple is to move in a tumbling, rippling way, as choppy water heaves up and down.

clue.text: Stale savour in old spiced wine, sweet, causing bad vibes?

indicators.note: in places the stale-savour word inside the spiced-wine word

blocks.note: piment is an old sweetened, spiced wine
resent once meant to savour or have a taste of; stale says the sense is obsolete

explanation.surface: Stale taste in old mulled wine produces a sense of unease.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stale' marks an obsolete sense of resent, to taste or savour; 'bad vibes' is a playful gloss, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: A presentiment is a foreboding that something unpleasant will happen, much like the uneasy feeling of bad vibes.

clue.text: Excuse dissipation? Not sure

indicators.note: not here means without, so the following word is taken off the longer one

blocks.note: a life of pleasure is one of dissipation
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether dissipation can be excused, and the answer is uncertain.
explanation.walkthrough: Take SURE away from PLEASURE to leave PLEA.
explanation.definitionFit: A plea can be an excuse or pretext offered in justification.

clue.text: Type of stone wall parish shortly has to renew mortar in

indicators.note: shortly says the word is cut short, keeping only its opening letters

blocks.note: the first three letters of parish, also its abbreviation
to point brickwork is to fill the joints with fresh mortar

explanation.surface: The parish must repoint a stone wall of a particular type.
explanation.definitionFit: Parpoint, or perpend, is a stone running through the full thickness of a wall, giving a kind of stone wall construction.

clue.text: Big car, muddy, old, but not unserviceable

indicators.note: but not means except for, so the unserviceable letters are excluded from the longer word

blocks.note: limous is an obsolete word for muddy or slimy
U/S is the abbreviation for unserviceable

explanation.surface: A large car, old and muddy, still runs.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove US from LIMOUS to leave LIMO.
explanation.definitionFit: A limo is short for limousine, a large luxurious car.

clue.text: Prelude: middle section without start of coda beginning to end

indicators.note: without means lacking, so the coda's initial is dropped from the middle word
start of points to the first letter of the next word only
beginning points to the opening letter of the word after it

blocks.note: the middle section of something is its centre
the first letter of coda
the first letter of end

explanation.surface: A musical prelude whose middle section lacks the start of the coda that brings the piece to an end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prelude' and 'coda' set a musical scene, but entrée here is a general word for an introduction.
explanation.definitionFit: An entrée is an entry or introduction, and in music an introductory piece, so it works as a prelude.

clue.text: One taking to the water for Leander content to feather oar

definitions.text: One taking to the water for Leander

indicators.note: content means what is held inside, so the answer is inside the next words

blocks.note: the end of feather joined to the start of oar

explanation.surface: A Leander club rower is happy to feather the oar.
explanation.walkthrough: Leander is a famous rowing club at Henley, but here he is the Greek lover who swam the Hellespont nightly to Hero; she drowned herself after he died.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth Hero leapt into the sea out of grief for her lover Leander, so she took to the water for him.

clue.text: 'What's this?' the old grumble distinctly

blocks.note: first meaning: an archaic verb for complain
second meaning: clearly

explanation.walkthrough: The quoted question models a grumble; 'the old' marks the sense as archaic.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain was once a verb meaning to lament or complain, and as an adverb it means clearly or distinctly.

clue.text: Canoeist perished — may we decorate graveyard?

indicators.note: something perished has decayed and fallen apart, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A canoeist has died; mourners ask if they may decorate the churchyard.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a question asked by the flowers themselves, the plural 'we' matching the plural answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Winter aconites are small yellow flowers often naturalised in churchyards, carpeting graves in early spring.

clue.text: Pit leaders from Kimberley hoarding uncut diamonds

indicators.note: leaders are the front runners, so the initial letter of each word is taken

blocks.note: the initial letters of the four words

explanation.surface: Mine bosses at Kimberley are stockpiling uncut diamonds.
explanation.walkthrough: Kimberley in South Africa is famous for its diamond mines, which feeds the picture of a pit.
explanation.definitionFit: A khud is an Anglo-Indian word for a pit, ravine or hollow.

clue.text: Relish fool's gold

blocks.note: a sap is a fool; the 's joins it to the next piece
or is gold in heraldry

explanation.surface: A sardonic remark that someone enjoys iron pyrites, the fake 'fool's gold'.
explanation.walkthrough: Fool's gold is iron pyrites, but the phrase splits into fool and gold.
explanation.definitionFit: Sapor is a word for taste or flavour, and relish likewise means a distinctive flavour.

clue.text: Bass mode adjusted to include piece of music for early woodwind

indicators.note: adjusted means altered or set differently, so these letters are rearranged
to include means to take something inside, so the music piece is placed within the rearranged letters

blocks.note: B is the abbreviation for bass
taken as written
a bar is a short section of a musical score

explanation.surface: A bass player's mode is adjusted to suit early woodwind music.
explanation.walkthrough: B and MODE rearranged give BOMDE, with BAR inserted: BOM(BAR)DE.
explanation.definitionFit: A bombarde is a medieval and Renaissance shawm, a loud double-reed instrument, the ancestor of the oboe.

clue.text: Former triumph over, cower wretchedly in tangle

indicators.note: wretchedly suggests something in a sorry, disordered state, so the letters are rearranged
in places the rearranged letters inside the tangle word

blocks.note: tangle and ore are both kinds of seaweed
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone once victorious now cowers miserably in a mess.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tangle' looks like a mess but is a seaweed, and ore is another name for seaweed.
explanation.definitionFit: Orecrowe is Spenser's form of overcrow, to crow over or triumph over someone, an archaic word.

clue.text: Hardy shrub, one found in rocky height and in equal quantities below

indicators.note: found in places the one letter inside the rocky height word
below in a down clue means the next piece follows underneath the first

blocks.note: a crag is a steep rugged rock
a means one
ana, on prescriptions, means of each the same quantity

explanation.surface: A hardy shrub grows on a rocky height, with equal amounts further down.
explanation.walkthrough: Ana is the pharmacists' term, from Greek, written on prescriptions for 'of each, in equal quantities'.
explanation.definitionFit: Caragana is a genus of tough leguminous shrubs, such as the Siberian pea tree, noted for withstanding cold.

clue.text: Anti-asthma drug disturbed poise of kidneys in being injected

indicators.note: disturbed means upset or thrown out of order, so the poise letters are rearranged
being injected means put inside, so the kidneys phrase goes into the rearranged letters

blocks.note: taken as written
renal means relating to the kidneys
taken as written

explanation.surface: An asthma drug upsets one's balance, especially when the kidneys are injected.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is not a link here: it joins the kidneys word so that both go inside together.
explanation.definitionFit: Isoprenaline is a bronchodilator once widely prescribed to relieve asthma attacks.

clue.text: Protesters upset mentors with angry tirades

indicators.note: upset means overturned or thrown into disorder, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
rants are angry tirades

explanation.surface: Protesters have upset their mentors by ranting angrily.
explanation.definitionFit: Remonstrants are those who make a formal protest or objection, so protesters is a synonym.

clue.text: Short swim after climbing in head waters, turbulent

indicators.note: climbing in a down clue means going upwards, so the word reads from bottom to top
in places the swim word inside the head word

blocks.note: ras is a headland or cape
a dip is a brief swim

explanation.surface: After climbing, a short swim in the headwaters, which are rough.
explanation.walkthrough: 'head waters' looks like one unit, but 'head' belongs to the wordplay and 'waters, turbulent' is the definition. Ras is an Arabic-derived word for a headland.
explanation.definitionFit: Rapids are stretches of a river where the current runs fast over rocks, making the water turbulent.

clue.text: Live artist dispenses with one around picture's finishing touch?

definitions.text: Live artist dispenses with one around picture's finishing touch?

indicators.note: dispenses with means does without, so the one is dropped from the artist word
around suggests turning about, so the remaining letters are spun into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
a means one
the last letter of picture

explanation.surface: A painter does without a live model except for the final touches to the picture.
explanation.walkthrough: ARTIST loses A to leave RTIST, and with E the letters are rearranged. The whole clue also describes the answer: the live subject an artist needs on hand for the finishing touches.
explanation.definitionFit: A sitter is the person who poses for a portrait, the living model before the painter.

clue.text: Feature of rock gardens? Nurse round misshapen tuber

indicators.note: round means surrounding, so the nurse word goes about the other letters
misshapen means put out of its proper form, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: aia, or ayah, is an Indian nursemaid
taken as written

explanation.surface: A gardener nurses a deformed tuber in the rockery.
explanation.walkthrough: Aia, or ayah, is an Anglo-Indian word for a nursemaid, a crossword favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: Aubretia is a trailing purple-flowered plant commonly grown spilling over rocks and walls in rock gardens.

clue.text: Nary a cry goes up for this particular item

indicators.note: goes up in a down clue means rising from bottom to top, so the letters read backwards

blocks.note: nary means not one, so no sob

explanation.surface: Nobody cries out for this particular thing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'particular' hides 'particle': the definition is a pun on a particle item.
explanation.definitionFit: A boson is a type of subatomic particle, so a punning 'particle-ar' item.

clue.text: Cert last in race? Criticism results

indicators.note: last in points to the final letter of the following word only

blocks.note: a snip is a certainty, a sure thing
the final letter of race

explanation.surface: A racing tip comes last, and criticism follows.
explanation.walkthrough: Cert is British slang for a certainty, typically a horse sure to win; snip means the same.
explanation.definitionFit: To snipe is to make sly critical attacks, and as a noun a snipe is such a jibe.

clue.text: Positive meaning to seize upon in Shakespeare

blocks.note: P is the abbreviation for positive
the hang of something is its meaning, as in getting the hang

explanation.surface: Positive meaning is something to grasp in Shakespeare.
explanation.definitionFit: Phang is Shakespeare's spelling of fang, used as a verb to mean seize or grip with the teeth.

clue.text: Riot that's violent, about nothing

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the violent word goes around the nothing

blocks.note: hot can mean violent or fiery
O represents nothing, zero

explanation.surface: A violent riot breaks out over nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Riot' suggests violence, but it is meant in the sense of something hilarious.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoot and a riot are both informal terms for a very funny person or occasion.

clue.text: Fellow laid up, given drug for swelling

indicators.note: laid up in a down clue suggests turned upwards, so the word reads from bottom to top

blocks.note: a don is a fellow of a university college
E is slang for ecstasy

explanation.surface: A sick fellow is given medicine for a swelling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Laid up' suggests illness, but here it says the word goes upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A node is a knob or swelling, as on a joint or a lymph gland.

clue.text: Jumping onto part of Indian train?

definitions.text: Jumping onto part of Indian train?

indicators.note: jumping suggests leaping about, so the letters hop into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A passenger leaps aboard a carriage of an Indian railway train.
explanation.walkthrough: The train is not a railway train but a caravan of pack animals that riders mount.
explanation.definitionFit: An oont is an Anglo-Indian word for a camel, one of the animals in a camel train that one jumps onto.

clue.text: Portion of Scotch beef? Minced rib steak

indicators.note: minced meat is chopped up small, so the letters are cut up and rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A cut of Aberdeen Angus beef is minced from a rib steak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scotch beef' suggests the meat, but the portion is the breast of the body and Scotch marks the dialect word.
explanation.definitionFit: Breaskit is a Scots form of breast, a portion of a beef carcass, with the question mark flagging the pun.

clue.text: Dry recipe replaced by rum butter in Scotland? Probably not!

indicators.note: replaced by means one item swaps out for another in the word

blocks.note: taken as written
R is the abbreviation for recipe, as on a prescription
rum means odd or strange

explanation.surface: A dry recipe in which rum butter is swapped in, for a Scottish dessert.
explanation.walkthrough: In DRY, R gives way to ODD: D-ODD-Y. 'Rum butter' looks like the brandy-butter sauce, but rum and butter separate.
explanation.definitionFit: A doddy is a Scots name for a hornless cow, which cannot butt, so it is unlikely to be a butter.

clue.text: A jug of retsina, say, load of Argive plonk? The reverse

indicators.note: a load is what is carried inside, so the answer is contained within the words
the reverse says the letters must be read from right to left

blocks.note: spans the end of Argive and the start of plonk

explanation.surface: A jug of retsina is a load of Greek plonk, or maybe the other way round.
explanation.walkthrough: Argive means from Argos, in Greece. Retsina is a resinated Greek wine.
explanation.definitionFit: An olpe is an ancient Greek jug with a pinched lip, used for pouring wine such as retsina.

clue.text: Stuff on board, set out before the day's ending

indicators.note: out means disordered or out of place, so the set letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
eve is the end of the day, evening

explanation.surface: The cargo is loaded aboard and the ship sets out before nightfall.
explanation.walkthrough: SET rearranged gives STE, followed by EVE.
explanation.definitionFit: To steeve is to stow cargo tightly in a ship's hold, packing it on board.

clue.text: LGV transporting liquid in tons, old measure

blocks.note: T is the abbreviation for tons
an anker is an old liquid measure of about ten gallons

explanation.surface: A heavy goods vehicle carrying tons of liquid, measured the old-fashioned way.
explanation.walkthrough: LGV is the British abbreviation for large goods vehicle, a lorry or truck.
explanation.definitionFit: A tanker is a road vehicle built to carry bulk liquids, a type of large goods vehicle.
